chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter X
paragraphs: Prince Andrew stayed in Brünn with Bilíbin, a Russian he knew from the diplomatic service.

"Ah, my dear Prince! I couldn't ask for a more welcome guest," said Bilíbin, coming out to meet Prince Andrew. "Franz, put the prince's things in my bedroom," he told the servant who was showing Bolkónski in. "So you're a bearer of victory news? Wonderful! And here I am sitting around sick, as you can see."
After washing and changing, Prince Andrew came into the diplomat's luxurious study and sat down to the dinner that had been prepared for him. Bilíbin settled himself comfortably by the fire.

After his journey and the campaign, during which he'd been deprived of every comfort of cleanliness and refinement, Prince Andrew felt a pleasant sense of ease among the luxurious surroundings he'd been accustomed to since childhood. Beyond that, it was pleasant—after his reception by the Austrians—to speak, if not in Russian (they were speaking French), at least with a Russian who would, he assumed, share the general Russian hostility toward the Austrians that was particularly intense at the time.

Bilíbin was a thirty-five-year-old bachelor who moved in the same circles as Prince Andrew. They'd known each other previously in Petersburg but had become closer when Prince Andrew was in Vienna with Kutúzov. Just as Prince Andrew was a young man who showed every sign of rising high in the military, so Bilíbin—to an even greater extent—showed every sign of rising in the diplomatic world. He was still young but no longer a novice diplomat, having entered the service at sixteen and served in Paris and Copenhagen before landing a fairly important post in Vienna. Both the foreign minister and the Russian ambassador in Vienna knew him and valued him. He wasn't one of those many diplomats who are respected merely because they have certain negative qualities, avoid doing certain things, and speak French. He was one of those who genuinely enjoyed work and knew how to do it well, and despite his natural laziness would sometimes spend an entire night at his desk. He worked well regardless of the subject matter. It wasn't the question "What for?" but "How?" that interested him. He didn't particularly care what a diplomatic matter was about, but it gave him enormous pleasure to craft a circular, memorandum, or report with skill, precision, and elegance. Bilíbin's services were valued not only for his writing but also for his ability to deal and converse with people in the highest spheres.

Bilíbin enjoyed conversation the way he enjoyed work—only when it could be made elegantly witty. In society he was always waiting for a chance to say something memorable and only joined a conversation when such an opportunity arose. His talk was always laced with cleverly original, polished phrases of general interest. These sayings were prepared in the inner workshop of his mind in portable form, as if designed so that minor society figures could carry them from one drawing room to the next. And indeed, Bilíbin's witticisms circulated through the Viennese salons and often had an influence on matters considered important.

His thin, worn, sallow face was covered with deep wrinkles that always looked as clean and well-scrubbed as fingertips after a long bath. The movement of these wrinkles was the principal means of expression on his face. His forehead would furrow into deep folds with his eyebrows raised, then his eyebrows would drop and deep creases would form on his cheeks. His small, deep-set eyes always sparkled and looked straight at you.
"Well, tell me about your exploits," he said.
Bolkónski, very modestly and without once mentioning himself, described the battle and his reception by the Minister of War.
"They received me and my news the way you'd receive a dog that wanders into a bowling alley," he concluded.
Bilíbin smiled and the wrinkles on his face disappeared.

[Speaking in French] "However, my dear fellow," he remarked, examining his nails from a distance and puckering the skin above his left eye, "despite the deep respect I hold for the Orthodox Russian army, I must confess that your victory was not exactly the most victorious of victories."
[The above was spoken in French.]
He went on talking this way in French, switching to Russian only for words he wanted to make contemptuous.
"Come now! You fell on the unfortunate Mortier with your entire force—his single division—and even then Mortier slipped through your fingers! Where's the victory in that?"
"But seriously," said Prince Andrew, "we can at least say without boasting that it was somewhat better than Ulm..."
"Why didn't you capture even one marshal for us?"

"Because things don't always go according to plan or unfold with parade-ground precision. We expected, as I told you, to reach their rear by seven in the morning but didn't get there until five in the afternoon."
"And why didn't you get there at seven in the morning? You should have been there by seven," returned Bilíbin with a smile. "You should have been there at seven in the morning."
"Why didn't you manage to convince Bonaparte through diplomatic channels to leave Genoa alone?" retorted Prince Andrew in the same tone.

"I know," interrupted Bilíbin, "you're thinking it's very easy to capture marshals while sitting on a sofa by the fire! That's true enough, but still—why didn't you capture him? So don't be surprised if not only the Minister of War but also His Most August Majesty Emperor and King Francis isn't exactly thrilled by your victory. Even I, a lowly secretary of the Russian Embassy, feel no need to celebrate by giving my Franz a coin or letting him go off to the Prater with his sweetheart... Though of course, we don't have a Prater here."
He looked Prince Andrew straight in the eye and suddenly smoothed his forehead.

"Now it's my turn to ask you 'why?' my dear fellow," said Bolkónski. "I confess I don't understand—perhaps there are diplomatic subtleties here beyond my humble intelligence—but I can't make sense of it. Mack loses an entire army, Archduke Ferdinand and Archduke Karl show no signs of life and blunder after blunder. Kutúzov alone wins a real victory, breaking the spell of French invincibility, and the Minister of War doesn't even want to hear the details."

"That's exactly the point, my dear fellow. You see, it's all 'hurrah for the Tsar, for Russia, for the Orthodox faith!' That's all very well, but what do we—I mean the Austrian court—care about your victories? Bring us good news of a victory by Archduke Karl or Ferdinand—one archduke's as good as another, as you know—even if it's only over a fire brigade of Bonaparte's, and that would be another story entirely: we'd fire off cannons! But this kind of thing seems designed to annoy us. Archduke Karl does nothing, Archduke Ferdinand disgraces himself. You abandon Vienna, give up its defense—as if to say: 'God is with us, but you and your capital are on your own!' The one general we all loved—Schmidt—you get killed by a bullet, and then you congratulate us on the victory! Admit it: more irritating news than yours could hardly be imagined. It's as though it were done on purpose, completely on purpose. Besides, suppose you did win a brilliant victory—even if Archduke Karl had won one—what difference would it make to the overall course of events? It's too late now that Vienna is occupied by the French army!"
"What? Occupied? Vienna occupied?"
"Not only occupied—Bonaparte is at Schönbrunn, and the count, our dear Count Vrbna, goes to him for his orders."
After the exhaustion of the journey, his reception, and especially after dinner, Bolkónski found he could not fully grasp the significance of what he was hearing.

"Count Lichtenfels was here this morning," Bilíbin continued, "and showed me a letter describing the French parade through Vienna in full detail: Prince Murat and the whole spectacle... So you see, your victory is hardly cause for celebration, and you can't expect to be received as a savior."

"Honestly, I don't care about that. I really don't care at all," said Prince Andrew, beginning to realize that his news of the battle near Krems was truly insignificant compared to something like the fall of Austria's capital. "But how was Vienna taken? What about the bridge and its famous fortifications? What about Prince Auersperg? We'd heard that Prince Auersperg was defending Vienna."

"Prince Auersperg is on this side of the river—our side—and he's defending us. Doing it rather badly, I'd say, but still defending us. Vienna, though, is on the other side. No, the bridge hasn't been taken yet, and I hope it won't be, since it's been mined and orders have been given to blow it up. Otherwise we'd have long since been in the Bohemian mountains, and you and your army would have had a very bad time caught between two fires."
"But this still doesn't mean the campaign is over," said Prince Andrew.

"Well, I think it is. The big men here think so too, but they don't dare say it. It will be as I said at the start of the campaign: it won't be your skirmish at Dürrenstein, or gunpowder at all, that decides this—but the people who planned it," said Bilíbin, quoting one of his own bon mots, releasing the wrinkles on his forehead, and pausing. "The only question now is what comes of the meeting between Emperor Alexander and the King of Prussia in Berlin. If Prussia joins the allies, Austria's hand will be forced and there will be war. If not, it's just a matter of deciding where to draw up the terms of the new Campo Formio."
"What an extraordinary genius!" Prince Andrew suddenly exclaimed, clenching his small fist and striking the table. "And what luck the man has!"

"Bonaparte?" said Bilíbin inquiringly, wrinkling his forehead to signal that a witticism was coming. "Buonaparte?" he repeated, stressing the 'u.' "I think, however, now that he's laying down the law for Austria at Schönbrunn, we really must drop the 'u.' I shall certainly adopt the innovation and simply call him Bonaparte!"
[Bilíbin's joke: "We must let him off the 'u'!" — a pun on the French spelling of Buonaparte vs. Bonaparte.]
"But joking aside," said Prince Andrew, "do you really think the campaign is over?"

"Here's what I think. Austria has been made a fool of, and she's not used to it. She'll retaliate. And she's been made a fool of in the first place because her provinces have been pillaged—they say the holy Russian army loots terribly—her army is destroyed, her capital taken, and all this for the sake of His Sardinian Majesty's lovely eyes. And therefore—this is just between us—I have an instinctive feeling that we're being deceived. My instinct tells me there are negotiations with France going on, and plans for peace—a secret, separate peace."
["Lovely eyes" — from the French expression "beaux yeux," meaning for someone's sake, implying an unworthy cause.]
"Impossible!" cried Prince Andrew. "That would be too despicable."
"If we live, we'll see," replied Bilíbin, his face becoming smooth again—a sign the conversation was over.

When Prince Andrew reached the room prepared for him and lay down in a clean shirt on the feather bed with its warm, fragrant pillows, he felt that the battle whose news he'd brought was far, far away from him. The alliance with Prussia, Austria's treachery, Bonaparte's latest triumph, tomorrow's levee and parade, and his audience with Emperor Francis occupied his thoughts.

He closed his eyes, and immediately a roar of cannon fire, musketry, and the rattling of carriage wheels seemed to fill his ears, and once again in his mind the musketeers were descending the hill in a thin line, the French were firing, and he felt his heart pounding as he rode forward beside Schmidt with bullets whistling cheerfully all around. He experienced the joy of being alive tenfold, as he hadn't since childhood.
He woke up...
"Yes, all of that really happened!" he said, and smiling to himself like a happy child, he fell into a deep, youthful sleep.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter XI
paragraphs: The next day he woke late. As his recent impressions came flooding back, the first thought in his mind was that today he had to be presented to Emperor Francis. He remembered the Minister of War, the courteous Austrian adjutant, Bilíbin, and last night's conversation. Having dressed in full parade uniform—which he hadn't worn in a long time—he went into Bilíbin's study looking fresh, lively, and handsome, with his hand still bandaged. Four gentlemen from the diplomatic corps were already in the study. Prince Andrew was already acquainted with Prince Hippolyte Kurágin, who served as a secretary to the embassy. Bilíbin introduced him to the others.

The gentlemen gathered at Bilíbin's were young, wealthy, fashionable men who formed a special circle both here and in Vienna. Bilíbin, their leader, called the group "ours." This set, made up almost entirely of diplomats, clearly had its own interests that had nothing to do with war or politics but revolved around high society, certain women, and the ceremonial side of government service. These gentlemen welcomed Prince Andrew as one of their own—an honor they extended to very few. Out of politeness, and to start a conversation, they asked him a few questions about the army and the battle, but then the talk quickly turned to lighthearted jokes and gossip.
"Ours."

"But the best part was," said one, telling the story of a fellow diplomat's misfortune, "that the Chancellor told him point-blank that his posting to London was a promotion and that he should treat it as such. Can you imagine the look on his face?"
"But the worst of it, gentlemen—and I'm giving Kurágin away here—is that the man is genuinely suffering, and this Don Juan, this scoundrel, is taking advantage of it!"
Prince Hippolyte was sprawled in a lounge chair with his legs thrown over the armrest. He started laughing.
"Tell me about that!" he said.
"Oh, you Don Juan! You snake!" cried several voices.

"You don't know this yet, Bolkónski," said Bilíbin, turning to Prince Andrew, "but all the horrors committed by the French army—I almost said the Russian army—are nothing compared to what this man has been doing to the women here!"
[Speaking in French] "Woman is man's companion," announced Prince Hippolyte, peering through a lorgnette at his own elevated legs.
"Woman is man's companion."

Bilíbin and the rest of "ours" burst out laughing right in Hippolyte's face, and Prince Andrew saw that Hippolyte—of whom, he had to admit, he had nearly been jealous on his wife's account—was the group's favorite target.
"Oh, I have to give you a treat," Bilíbin whispered to Bolkónski. "Kurágin is priceless when he talks politics—you have to see how serious he gets!"
He sat down next to Hippolyte, furrowed his brow, and began talking to him about politics. Prince Andrew and the others gathered around the two of them.

[Speaking in French] "The Berlin cabinet cannot express a sentiment of alliance," Hippolyte began, looking around importantly at the others, "without expressing... as in its last note... you understand... Besides, unless His Majesty the Emperor departs from the principle of our alliance..."

"Wait, I'm not finished..." he said to Prince Andrew, grabbing him by the arm. "I believe that intervention will prove stronger than non-intervention. And..." He paused. "Finally, one cannot attribute the non-receipt of our dispatch of November eighteenth. That is how it will end." And he released Bolkónski's arm to show he had quite finished.
"Demosthenes, I recognize you by the pebble hidden in your golden mouth!" said Bilíbin, and the tuft of hair on his head bobbed with satisfaction.
Everyone laughed, and Hippolyte louder than anyone. He was clearly embarrassed and breathing hard, but he couldn't contain the wild laughter that contorted his normally blank features.

"Well then, gentlemen," said Bilíbin, "Bolkónski is my guest here in this house and in Brünn itself. I want to show him the best time I can, with all the pleasures life here has to offer. If we were in Vienna it would be easy, but here in this miserable Moravian backwater it's harder, and I'm asking all of you to help me. You can handle the theater, I'll take care of society, and you, Hippolyte—the women, naturally."
"We absolutely must introduce him to Amelie—she's divine!" said one of "ours," kissing his fingertips.
"In general, we need to convert this bloodthirsty soldier to more civilized pursuits," said Bilíbin.
"I'm afraid I won't be able to take advantage of your hospitality, gentlemen. It's already time for me to go," replied Prince Andrew, glancing at his watch.
"Where to?"
"To see the Emperor."
"Oh! Oh! Oh!"
"Well, goodbye, Bolkónski! Goodbye, Prince! Come back early for dinner," called several voices. "We'll look after you."
"When you're speaking with the Emperor, try to say good things about the supply situation and the route planning," said Bilíbin, walking him to the hall.
"I'd like to speak well of them, but as far as I know the facts, I can't," replied Bolkónski with a smile.
"Well, talk as much as you can anyway. He has a passion for giving audiences, but he doesn't like talking himself and can't manage it, as you'll see."

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter XII
paragraphs: At the levee, Prince Andrew stood among the Austrian officers as instructed, and Emperor Francis merely stared fixedly at his face and gave a slight nod with his long head. But after it was over, the adjutant he'd seen the day before ceremoniously informed Bolkónski that the Emperor wished to grant him an audience. Emperor Francis received him standing in the middle of the room. Before the conversation began, Prince Andrew was struck by the fact that the Emperor seemed flustered and kept blushing, as if he didn't know what to say.
"Tell me, when did the battle begin?" he asked hastily.

Prince Andrew answered. Then came more questions, equally straightforward: "Was Kutúzov in good health? When had he left Krems?" The Emperor spoke as though his only goal were to get through a set number of questions—the answers, quite obviously, didn't interest him.
"At what time did the battle begin?" the Emperor asked.

"I cannot inform Your Majesty at what time the battle began at the front lines, but at Dürrenstein, where I was stationed, our attack began after five in the afternoon," replied Bolkónski, growing more animated and expecting he might finally have the chance to give a reliable account—which he had prepared in his mind—of all he knew and had seen. But the Emperor smiled and cut him off.
"How many miles?"
"From where to where, Your Majesty?"
"From Dürrenstein to Krems."
"Three and a half miles, Your Majesty."
"The French have abandoned the left bank?"
"According to the scouts, the last of them crossed on rafts during the night."
"Is there sufficient forage in Krems?"
"Forage has not been supplied to the extent—"
The Emperor cut him off.
"At what time was General Schmidt killed?"
"At seven o'clock, I believe."
"At seven o'clock? That is very sad, very sad!"

The Emperor thanked Prince Andrew and bowed. Prince Andrew withdrew and was immediately surrounded on all sides by courtiers. Everywhere he saw friendly faces and heard kind words. Yesterday's adjutant reproached him for not having stayed at the palace and offered him the use of his own house. The Minister of War came up to congratulate him on the Order of Maria Theresa, third class, which the Emperor was bestowing on him. The Empress's chamberlain invited him to see Her Majesty. The archduchess also wished to see him. He didn't know whom to respond to first and took a few seconds to collect his thoughts. Then the Russian ambassador took him by the shoulder, led him to the window, and began talking.

Contrary to Bilíbin's prediction, the news Prince Andrew had brought was received with joy. A thanksgiving service was arranged, Kutúzov was awarded the Grand Cross of Maria Theresa, and the entire army received decorations. Bolkónski was invited everywhere and had to spend the whole morning making calls on the leading Austrian dignitaries. Between four and five in the afternoon, having completed all his calls, he was walking back to Bilíbin's house, composing in his head a letter to his father about the battle and his visit to Brünn. At the door he found a carriage half-loaded with luggage. Franz, Bilíbin's servant, was struggling to drag a heavy trunk out through the front door.
Before returning to Bilíbin's, Prince Andrew had stopped at a bookshop to stock up on books for the campaign and had spent some time browsing.
"What's going on?" he asked.
"Oh, Your Excellency!" said Franz, wrestling the trunk toward the carriage. "We have to move on again. That scoundrel is at our heels!"
"What? What do you mean?" asked Prince Andrew.
Bilíbin came out to meet him. His usually calm face showed excitement.
"There now! You have to admit this is delightful," he said. "The Thabor Bridge affair, in Vienna... They've crossed it without firing a shot!"
Prince Andrew couldn't grasp what he meant.
"Where have you been that you don't know what every cab driver in town knows?"
"I've been at the archduchess's. I heard nothing there."
"And you didn't notice that everyone is packing up?"
"I didn't... What's this all about?" Prince Andrew asked impatiently.

"What's it about? The French have crossed the bridge that Auersperg was supposed to be defending, and the bridge was not blown up. So now Murat is racing down the road toward Brünn and will be here in a day or two."
"What? Here? But why didn't they blow up the bridge if it was mined?"
"That's exactly what I'd like to know. Nobody—not even Bonaparte himself—can explain it."
Bolkónski shrugged.
"But if the bridge has been crossed, it means the army is lost too. It'll be cut off," he said.

"That's precisely the situation," answered Bilíbin. "Listen. The French entered Vienna as I told you. Fine. The next day—which was yesterday—these gentlemen, the marshals Murat, Lannes, and Belliard, mount their horses and ride to the bridge. (Note that all three are Gascons.) 'Gentlemen,' says one of them, 'you know the Thabor Bridge is mined and double-mined, that there are serious fortifications at the bridgehead, and that fifteen thousand men have orders to blow it up and keep us from crossing. But it would please our sovereign Emperor Napoleon if we took this bridge, so let's go take it!' 'Yes, let's!' say the others. And off they go and take the bridge, cross it, and now their entire army is on this side of the Danube, marching toward us—toward you, and your supply lines."
"The marshals."
"Stop joking," said Prince Andrew, sadly and seriously. The news pained him, and yet at the same time he was pleased.

The moment he learned that the Russian army was in such a desperate position, it occurred to him that he was the one destined to lead it out of this crisis—that here was the Toulon that would lift him from the ranks of obscure officers and offer him his first step toward glory! As he listened to Bilíbin, he was already imagining how, upon reaching the army, he would present an opinion at the war council—the only plan that could save them—and how he alone would be entrusted with carrying it out.
"Stop the joking," he said.

"I'm not joking," Bilíbin went on. "Nothing could be more true or more tragic. These gentlemen ride onto the bridge alone, waving white handkerchiefs. They assure the officer on duty that they, the marshals, are on their way to negotiate with Prince Auersperg. He lets them into the bridgehead. They spin a thousand tall tales, saying the war is over, that Emperor Francis is arranging a meeting with Bonaparte, that they'd like to see Prince Auersperg, and so on. The officer sends for Auersperg. The gentlemen embrace the Austrian officers, crack jokes, sit on the cannons, and meanwhile a French battalion slips onto the bridge unnoticed, throws the detonation charges into the water, and reaches the fortifications. At last the lieutenant general himself appears—our dear Prince Auersperg von Mautern. 'Dearest enemy! Flower of the Austrian army! Hero of the Turkish wars! Hostilities are over, we can shake hands... Emperor Napoleon burns with impatience to make Prince Auersperg's acquaintance.' In short, these gentlemen—true Gascons—so bewildered him with their fine words, and he was so flattered by his sudden intimacy with the French marshals, and so dazzled by the sight of Murat's cloak and ostrich plumes, that he couldn't see what was right in front of him—and forgot he was supposed to be firing on the enemy!" Despite his animated delivery, Bilíbin didn't forget to pause after this bon mot to let it land. "The French battalion rushes the bridgehead, spikes the guns, and the bridge is taken! But the best part," he continued, his excitement subsiding under the pleasant momentum of his own story, "is that the sergeant in charge of the cannon—the one meant to give the signal to detonate the mines—seeing the French troops swarming onto the bridge, was about to fire. But Lannes grabbed his hand. The sergeant, who was clearly smarter than his general, went up to Auersperg and said: 'Prince, you're being deceived—these are the French!' Murat, seeing that all was lost if the sergeant was allowed to speak, turned to Auersperg with a look of feigned astonishment—a true Gascon—and said: 'I hardly recognize the world-famous Austrian discipline when you allow a subordinate to address you like that!' It was a stroke of genius. Prince Auersperg, feeling his authority challenged, ordered the sergeant arrested. Come on, you have to admit this Thabor Bridge business is magnificent! It's not exactly stupidity, and it's not exactly treachery either..."
"Bridgehead."
"That their fire gets into his eyes and he forgets that he ought to be firing at the enemy."
"It might be treachery," said Prince Andrew, vividly picturing the gray overcoats, the wounds, the gunpowder smoke, the sounds of battle, and the glory that awaited him.

"Not that either. That would put the court in too bad a light," replied Bilíbin. "It's not treachery, not villainy, not stupidity—it's just like Ulm... it's..." He seemed to be searching for the right expression. "It's... it's a case of Mack. We've been Macked," he concluded, feeling he had produced a fresh witticism that would make the rounds. His previously furrowed brow smoothed out with pleasure, and with a slight smile he began examining his nails.
"Where are you off to?" he said suddenly to Prince Andrew, who had risen and was heading toward his room.
"I'm leaving."
"Where?"
"To the army."
"But you were planning to stay two more days."
"Now I'm leaving at once."
And Prince Andrew, after giving instructions for his departure, went to his room.
"You know, my dear fellow," said Bilíbin, following him, "I've been thinking about you. Why are you going?"
And as proof of the finality of his opinion, all the wrinkles vanished from his face.
Prince Andrew looked at him questioningly and said nothing.
"Why are you going? I know you think it's your duty to gallop back to the army now that it's in danger. I understand. My dear fellow, it is heroism!"
"Not at all," said Prince Andrew.

"But as a philosopher, be a consistent one. Look at the other side of the question and you'll see that your duty is actually to take care of yourself. Leave the heroics to those who are no longer fit for anything else... You haven't been ordered to return, and you haven't been dismissed from here. So you can stay and go wherever our bad luck takes us. They say we're heading for Olmütz, and Olmütz is a perfectly decent town. You and I will travel comfortably in my carriage."
"Stop joking, Bilíbin," said Bolkónski.

"I'm speaking sincerely, as a friend! Think about it. Where are you going, and why, when you could stay here? You're facing one of two outcomes"—and the skin over his left temple puckered—"either you won't reach your regiment before peace is concluded, or you'll share in the defeat and disgrace of Kutúzov's entire army."
And Bilíbin smoothed his temple, feeling his dilemma was unanswerable.
"I can't argue about it," replied Prince Andrew coldly, though he was thinking: "I am going to save the army."
"My dear fellow, you are a hero!" said Bilíbin.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter XIII
paragraphs: That same night, after taking leave of the Minister of War, Bolkónski set off to rejoin the army, not knowing where he would find it and fearing he might be captured by the French on the way to Krems.

In Brünn, everyone connected to the court was packing up, and the heavy baggage had already been dispatched to Olmütz. Near Hetzelsdorf, Prince Andrew reached the main road along which the Russian army was moving at great speed and in complete disorder. The road was so clogged with wagons that it was impossible to get through in a carriage. Prince Andrew got a horse and a Cossack escort from a Cossack commander, and hungry and exhausted, threading his way past the baggage wagons, he rode in search of the commander in chief and his own luggage. The most alarming reports about the army's situation reached him as he went, and the sight of the troops in their chaotic retreat confirmed every rumor.

He remembered words from Bonaparte's address to his army at the beginning of the campaign: [Speaking in French] "That Russian army which English gold has transported from the ends of the earth—we shall make it share the same fate as the army at Ulm." These words awakened in him astonishment at his hero's genius, a sting of wounded pride, and a hope for glory. "And if all that's left is to die?" he thought. "Well, if it comes to that, I'll do it no worse than anyone else."
"That Russian army which has been brought from the ends of the earth by English gold, we shall cause to share the same fate—the fate of the army at Ulm."

He looked with contempt at the endless, chaotic mass of detachments, wagons, guns, artillery pieces, and still more baggage trains and vehicles of every kind, overtaking one another and blocking the muddy road three and sometimes four abreast. From all sides, in front and behind, as far as the ear could reach, came the rattle of wheels, the creaking of carts and gun carriages, the tramp of horses, the crack of whips, shouts, cursing from soldiers and orderlies and officers urging their horses on. Along both sides of the road lay fallen horses—some skinned, some not—and broken-down carts beside which solitary soldiers sat waiting for something. Other soldiers, breaking away from their units in groups, headed off to the nearby villages or returned from them dragging sheep, chickens, hay, and bulging sacks. On every uphill and downhill stretch the crowds grew denser and the shouting more frantic. Soldiers, sinking knee-deep in mud, pushed the guns and wagons with their own hands. Whips cracked, hooves slipped, harness straps snapped, and lungs were strained with shouting. The officers directing the march rode back and forth between the wagons. Their voices were barely audible over the uproar, and you could see from their faces that they had given up any hope of restoring order.
"Here's our beloved Orthodox Russian army," thought Bolkónski, remembering Bilíbin's words.

Wanting to find out where the commander in chief was, he rode up to a convoy. Coming straight toward him was a strange one-horse vehicle, obviously cobbled together by soldiers from whatever materials they could find—something between a cart, a buggy, and a carriage. A soldier was driving it, and behind the leather hood sat a woman wrapped in shawls. Prince Andrew rode up and was about to ask a soldier for directions when he was interrupted by the desperate screaming of the woman in the vehicle. An officer in charge of the transport column was beating the soldier who drove the woman's cart for trying to push ahead of the others, and his whip was landing on the vehicle's canvas cover. The woman shrieked piercingly. Seeing Prince Andrew, she leaned out from behind the cover and, waving her thin arms from beneath a woolen shawl, cried:

"Aide-de-camp! Aide-de-camp! For God's sake... protect me! What will become of us? I'm the wife of the doctor of the Seventh Chasseurs... They won't let us through, we've been left behind and lost our people..."
"I'll flatten you like a pancake!" shouted the angry officer at the soldier. "Turn back with your woman!"
"Aide-de-camp! Help me! What is happening?" screamed the doctor's wife.
"Let this cart through. Can't you see it's a woman?" said Prince Andrew, riding up to the officer.
The officer glanced at him, and without answering turned back to the soldier. "I'll teach you to push ahead!... Back!"
"Let them through, I said!" repeated Prince Andrew, his lips pressed tight.

"And who are you?" shouted the officer, turning on him in a state of drunken rage. "Who are you? Are you in command here? Eh? I'm in command here, not you! Get back or I'll flatten you like a pancake!" he repeated. The expression clearly pleased him.
"That was a nice put-down for the little aide-de-camp," came a voice from behind.

Prince Andrew saw that the officer was in that state of blind, drunken fury when a man doesn't know what he's saying. He realized that defending the doctor's wife in her ramshackle cart might expose him to what he dreaded more than anything in the world—ridicule. But his instinct drove him forward. Before the officer could finish his sentence, Prince Andrew, his face twisted with fury, rode straight at him and raised his riding whip.
"Let—them—through!"
The officer flung his arm in the air and hastily rode away.
"It's all the fault of these headquarters people—they're the ones causing this chaos," he muttered. "Do what you want."

Prince Andrew, without looking up, rode quickly away from the doctor's wife, who was calling him her savior. Recalling every detail of the humiliating scene with disgust, he galloped on to the village where he'd been told the commander in chief was located.

Reaching the village, he dismounted and went to the nearest house, hoping to rest even for a moment, eat something, and try to sort out the painful, tormenting thoughts swirling in his mind. "This isn't an army—it's a mob of scoundrels," he thought as he approached the window of the first house, when a familiar voice called out his name.
He turned around. Nesvítski's handsome face was looking out of a small window. Nesvítski, chewing something and moving his moist lips, was waving his arm and calling him over.
"Bolkónski! Bolkónski! Can't you hear me? Come here, quickly!" he shouted.

Going inside, Prince Andrew found Nesvítski and another adjutant eating. They spun around to face him, asking if he had any news. On their familiar faces he read alarm and anxiety. This was especially striking on Nesvítski's face, which was usually so cheerful.
"Where is the commander in chief?" asked Bolkónski.
"Here, in that house," answered the adjutant.
"Well, is it true? Peace and surrender?" asked Nesvítski.
"I was going to ask you. I know nothing except that I barely managed to get here."
"And us, my dear fellow! It's terrible! I was wrong to laugh at Mack—we're getting it even worse," said Nesvítski. "But sit down and have something to eat."
"You won't be able to find your baggage or anything else now, Prince. And God only knows where your man Peter is," said the other adjutant.
"Where is headquarters?"
"We're spending the night in Znaim."

"Well, I've managed to pack everything I need onto two horses," said Nesvítski. "They made up excellent packs for me—good enough to cross the Bohemian mountains. Things look grim, old friend! But what's wrong with you? You must be sick—you're shivering like that," he added, noticing Prince Andrew flinch as if from an electric shock.
"It's nothing," replied Prince Andrew.
He had just recalled his encounter with the doctor's wife and the transport officer.
"What is the commander in chief doing here?" he asked.
"I can't make it out at all," said Nesvítski.
"Well, all I can make out is that everything is dreadful, completely dreadful," said Prince Andrew, and he went off to the house where the commander in chief was staying.

Passing Kutúzov's carriage and the exhausted saddle horses of his entourage, with their Cossacks talking loudly together, Prince Andrew entered the hallway. Kutúzov himself, he was told, was inside with Prince Bagratión and Weyrother—the Austrian general who had replaced Schmidt. In the corridor, little Kozlóvski was squatting on his heels in front of a clerk. The clerk, with his sleeves rolled up, was scribbling furiously on an overturned tub. Kozlóvski's face looked haggard—he clearly hadn't slept all night either. He glanced at Prince Andrew without so much as a nod.
"Second line... have you written it?" he went on dictating to the clerk. "The Kiev Grenadiers, Podolian..."
"Can't write that fast, Your Honor," said the clerk, looking up at Kozlóvski with irritation and disrespect.

Through the door came the sounds of Kutúzov's voice—agitated and unhappy—broken by another voice, one Prince Andrew didn't recognize. From the sound of these voices, from Kozlóvski's distracted expression, from the clerk's rudeness, from the fact that both Kozlóvski and the clerk were squatting on the floor by a tub so close to the commander in chief, and from the noisy laughter of the Cossacks holding the horses by the window—from all of this, Prince Andrew sensed that something critical and catastrophic was about to happen.
He turned to Kozlóvski with urgent questions.
"One moment, Prince," said Kozlóvski. "Orders for Bagratión."
"What about a surrender?"
"Nothing of the sort. Orders are being drawn up for a battle."

Prince Andrew moved toward the door where the voices were coming from. Just as he was about to open it, the voices fell silent, the door swung open, and Kutúzov appeared in the doorway with his eagle nose and puffy face. Prince Andrew stood directly in front of him, but the expression in the commander in chief's one good eye showed he was so consumed by thoughts and worries that he didn't even register who was standing there. He stared straight at his adjutant's face without recognizing him.
"Well, have you finished?" he said to Kozlóvski.
"One moment, Your Excellency."
Bagratión, a lean middle-aged man of medium height with a firm, impassive face of Eastern features, emerged behind the commander in chief.
"I have the honor to present myself," said Prince Andrew, louder this time, holding out an envelope to Kutúzov.
"Ah, from Vienna? Very good. Later, later!"
Kutúzov walked out to the porch with Bagratión.
"Well, goodbye, Prince," he said to Bagratión. "My blessing, and may Christ be with you in your great endeavor!"

His face suddenly softened and tears welled in his eyes. With his left hand he drew Bagratión toward him, and with his right—on which he wore a ring—he made the sign of the cross over him in what was clearly a habitual gesture, offering his puffy cheek. But Bagratión kissed him on the neck instead.
"Christ be with you!" Kutúzov repeated, and turned toward his carriage. "Get in with me," he said to Bolkónski.
"Your Excellency, I would like to be of use here. Allow me to stay with Prince Bagratión's detachment."
"Get in," said Kutúzov, and when he noticed Bolkónski still hesitating, he added: "I need good officers myself. Need them myself!"
They got into the carriage and drove in silence for a few minutes.

"There is still much, much ahead of us," he said with the penetrating insight of an old man who seemed to understand everything passing through Bolkónski's mind. "If even a tenth of his detachment comes back, I shall thank God," he added, as if speaking to himself.

Prince Andrew glanced at Kutúzov's face, only a foot away, and found his eyes drawn to the carefully washed seams of the scar near his temple where a bullet had pierced his skull at Ismail, and to the empty eye socket. "Yes, he has earned the right to speak so calmly about those men's deaths," thought Bolkónski.
"That is why I ask to be sent to that detachment," he said.

Kutúzov did not answer. He seemed to have forgotten what he'd been saying and sat sunk in thought. Five minutes later, swaying gently on the soft springs of the carriage, he turned to Prince Andrew. There was not a trace of emotion on his face. With subtle irony, he began questioning Prince Andrew about the details of his interview with the Emperor, about the remarks he'd heard at court regarding the Krems affair, and about certain ladies they both knew.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter XIV
paragraphs: On November 1st, Kutúzov had received intelligence from a spy that the army he commanded was in a nearly hopeless situation. The spy reported that the French, having crossed the bridge at Vienna, were advancing in massive force toward Kutúzov's line of communication with the reinforcements arriving from Russia. If Kutúzov chose to remain at Krems, Napoleon's army of a hundred and fifty thousand men would completely cut him off and surround his exhausted force of forty thousand—and he would find himself in the same position as Mack at Ulm. If he chose to abandon the road connecting him with the approaching Russian reinforcements, he would have to march without roads into the unknown terrain of the Bohemian mountains, fighting off a superior enemy while giving up all hope of linking up with Buxhöwden. If he chose to retreat along the road from Krems to Olmütz to join the incoming Russian troops, he risked being overtaken on that road by the French who had crossed the Vienna bridge—and burdened by his baggage and supply trains, he would have to fight on the march against an enemy three times his strength attacking from two directions.
Kutúzov chose this last option.

The French, according to the spy, had crossed the Vienna bridge and were making forced marches toward Znaim, which lay sixty-six miles along Kutúzov's line of retreat. If he reached Znaim before the French, there was real hope of saving the army. If the French got there first, the entire army faced either the kind of humiliation Mack had suffered at Ulm, or total annihilation. But it was impossible for Kutúzov to reach Znaim ahead of the French with his whole army. The French road from Vienna to Znaim was shorter and better than the Russian road from Krems to Znaim.

The night he received this intelligence, Kutúzov sent Bagratión's advance guard—four thousand men—to the right, across the hills from the Krems-Znaim road to the Vienna-Znaim road. Bagratión was to make this march without stopping to rest and to take up a position facing Vienna with Znaim at his back. If he managed to get there ahead of the French, he was to hold them off for as long as possible. Kutúzov himself, with the rest of the army and all the supply trains, took the road to Znaim.

Marching thirty miles through a stormy night across trackless hills, with hungry, poorly shod soldiers, and losing a third of his men as stragglers along the way, Bagratión reached the Vienna-Znaim road at Hollabrünn a few hours ahead of the French approaching from Vienna. Kutúzov and his supply trains still had several days of marching before they could reach Znaim. So Bagratión, with his four thousand hungry, exhausted men, would have to hold off the entire enemy army for days at Hollabrünn—which was clearly impossible. But a twist of fate made the impossible possible. The success of the trick that had handed the Vienna bridge to the French without a fight led Murat to try deceiving Kutúzov in the same way. When Murat encountered Bagratión's small detachment on the Znaim road, he mistook it for Kutúzov's entire army. To ensure he could crush it completely, he waited for the rest of his troops still coming from Vienna, and in the meantime offered a three-day truce on the condition that both armies hold their positions without moving. Murat declared that peace negotiations were already underway, and that he was therefore proposing the truce to avoid unnecessary bloodshed. Count Nostitz, the Austrian general commanding the forward positions, believed Murat's envoy and pulled back, leaving Bagratión's division exposed. Another envoy rode to the Russian lines to announce the peace talks and offer the Russian army a three-day truce. Bagratión replied that he had no authority to accept or reject a truce and sent his adjutant to Kutúzov to report the offer.

A truce was Kutúzov's only chance to buy time, give Bagratión's worn-out troops some rest, and let the baggage and heavy supply trains—whose movements were hidden from the French—advance at least one more stage toward Znaim. The truce offer was the only chance, and a completely unexpected one, of saving the army. As soon as he received the news, Kutúzov immediately dispatched Adjutant General Wintzingerode to the enemy camp. Wintzingerode was not merely to agree to the truce but also to propose terms of surrender—and meanwhile, Kutúzov sent his adjutants racing back to push the movement of the entire army's baggage trains along the Krems-Znaim road as fast as possible. Bagratión's exhausted and hungry detachment, which alone was covering the movement of the supply trains and the whole army, had to remain in place facing an enemy eight times its size.

Kutúzov's expectation—that the surrender proposal (which committed him to nothing) would buy time for part of the transport to get through, and that Murat's mistake would soon be discovered—proved correct. As soon as Bonaparte, who was at Schönbrunn sixteen miles from Hollabrünn, received Murat's dispatch with the proposed truce and surrender terms, he saw through the ruse and wrote the following letter to Murat:
Schönbrunn, 25th Brumaire, 1805,
at eight o'clock in the morning
To PRINCE MURAT,

I cannot find words to express my displeasure. You command only my advance guard and have no right to arrange an armistice without my orders. You are costing me the fruits of a campaign. Break the armistice immediately and march on the enemy. Inform him that the general who signed that agreement had no authority to do so, and that no one but the Emperor of Russia has that right.

If, however, the Emperor of Russia ratifies that agreement, I will ratify it as well; but it is nothing more than a trick. March on, destroy the Russian army... You are in a position to seize its baggage and artillery.

The Russian Emperor's aide-de-camp is an impostor. Officers mean nothing when they have no authority; this one had none... The Austrians let themselves be fooled at the Vienna bridge crossing, and now you are letting yourself be fooled by an aide-de-camp of the Emperor.
NAPOLEON

Bonaparte's adjutant rode at full gallop with this furious letter to Murat. Bonaparte himself, not trusting his generals, moved out with the entire Guard toward the battlefield, determined not to let a ready victim escape. And Bagratión's four thousand men, meanwhile, cheerfully lit their campfires, dried and warmed themselves, and cooked porridge for the first time in three days—not one of them knowing or imagining what awaited them.
